Machine-learning methods are often called assumption-free. They make fewer assumptions
about the shape of a relationship than a linear model does, but they still assume the
data were collected in a way that lets the stations stand for the ocean. The five pages
in this section take each assumption in turn, on the same simulated survey as the rest
of the course. The first two cover what a model assumes about shape and spread, which
machine learning relaxes:

- **linearity and nonlinearity**: a linear model gives each input a fixed effect and a
  random forest does not; the forest finds the temperature curve that a straight line
  misses, yet still puts depth's peak in the wrong place;
- **distributional assumptions**: a random forest predicts skewed, unevenly spread
  counts without assuming a distribution, but its loss decides what it aims at, and
  trained on log counts it predicts too few animals.

The next two cover how the data were collected, which machine learning does not relax:

- **dependent data**: repeat visits to a site and neighbouring sites are worth fewer
  stations than their number, and resampling whole sites and whole areas measures how
  many fewer;
- **uneven sampling and extrapolation**: a model answers for conditions its survey never
  reached, and the distance to the nearest surveyed station shows where it is guessing.

The last page takes a rare answer:

- **class imbalance**: sensitivity, specificity and precision count misses and false
  alarms apart, and rebalancing the training data turns out to move the threshold.

The section picks up threads from earlier ones and passes some on.
[Distributional assumptions](distributional-assumptions.qmd) asks what each loss of
[Loss functions](../04-how-algorithms-learn/loss-functions.qmd) aims at.
[Splitting the data](../02-marine-data/splitting-data.qmd) kept each site's visits on one
side of the split; [Dependent data](dependent-data.qmd) measures what those visits are
worth, and [Spatial and temporal cross-validation](../07-validation/spatial-and-temporal-cv.qmd)
holds out whole areas.
[Uneven sampling and extrapolation](sampling-and-extrapolation.qmd) measures how far a
station lies from the survey as [k-nearest neighbours](../03-supervised-learning/nearest-neighbours.qmd)
finds its neighbours. [Class imbalance](class-imbalance.qmd) builds on the misses and
false alarms of [Logistic regression](../03-supervised-learning/logistic-regression.qmd)
and leaves whole-curve scores to
[Classification performance measures](../07-validation/classification-metrics.qmd).
A model that keeps one readable curve for each input waits for
[Black boxes and interpretable models](../10-interpretation/black-box-or-not.qmd).

## Further resources

**Documentation**

- [spatialsample](https://spatialsample.tidymodels.org/), tidymodels. Blocked, clustered and buffered resampling for data with a location, which is the concrete answer to most of this section.
- [Common pitfalls and recommended practices](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html), scikit-learn. Independence is assumed silently in almost every default, and this page says where.
